references.text: Moses cries out to the Lord in frustration over the people's complaints, just as he did at Rephidim. He asks what he should do with this difficult people.
The people threaten to stone Moses and Aaron, reflecting the same threat Moses feared at Rephidim.
David was in great distress because the people spoke of stoning him, just as Moses feared being stoned by the Israelites.
The people complained to Moses at the Red Sea, an earlier example of Israel's repeated complaints against Moses during their wilderness journey.
At Marah the people grumbled against Moses, and he cried out to the Lord, the same pattern that is repeated here at Rephidim.
The congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the Desert of Sin, yet another example of the people's repeated rebellion.
The Jews picked up stones to throw at Jesus, showing how stoning was a threat against God's appointed servants.
The Jews again picked up stones to stone Jesus, parallel to the threat Moses faced from the people.
Both verses illustrate the deep tension between the people and both Moses and God, where attacks on the leader express their disobedience to the Lord.
Both verses capture Moses' deeply personal crisis where he feels his mission has brought danger upon himself and the people, and he turns to God in despair.
The connection lies in Moses' expressed feeling that leading this people is an unbearable burden that threatens his life and mind.
Both verses show Moses as a mediator in a situation where the people have committed or are about to commit a great sin against God and His servant.
